pharm: A halogenated alkane (volatile liquid) vaporised and inhaled to produce dose-dependent general anaesthesia by central nervous system depression
quick: Titrated to effect by vaporiser; induction ~2-4% and maintenance ~0.5-1.5% in oxygen/nitrous oxide (MAC ~0.75% in O2)
Patient fasted per anaesthetic protocol; not orally administered
Crosses placenta and relaxes uterus; use only when clearly needed (e.g. obstetric anaesthesia by specialists)
Brief exposure; typically discard milk for a short period; specialist guidance
No specific dose change; little renal elimination
Avoid in prior halothane hepatitis or unexplained jaundice after prior exposure
Not applicable to acute anaesthetic use
Continuous anaesthetic/vital-sign monitoring; temperature (MH); postoperative LFTs if indicated
summary: Halothane is a volatile halogenated inhalational general anaesthetic used for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia, delivered via a calibrated vaporiser and titrated to clinical effect (MAC about 0.75% in oxygen). It is potent and non-irritant to airways, allowing smooth induction, but it sensitises the myocardium to catecholamines (arrhythmia risk), is a potent uterine relaxant, and produces dose-dependent cardiorespiratory depression. Its two principal serious hazards are halothane hepatitis - an immune-mediated, potentially fatal fulminant hepatic necrosis associated especially with repeated exposures - and malignant hyperthermia, for which halothane is a recognised triggering agent. Largely superseded in many countries by newer agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane), it remains in use in some settings. Repeat administration within a short interval should be avoided, and it is contraindicated where there is a history of halothane-associated hepatitis or jaundice or a personal/family history of malignant hyperthermia.
indications: Induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia

dosage.t: Inhalation via calibrated vaporiser in oxygen +/- nitrous oxide
dosage.n: Titrate to depth of anaesthesia and haemodynamics
Lower when combined with nitrous oxide/opioids

dosage.d: Titrated by vaporiser; MAC higher in infants/children
dosage.n: Administered only by trained anaesthetists with full monitoring

admin: Administer only by personnel trained in anaesthesia, using a calibrated vaporiser and equipment for assisted/controlled ventilation
Provide continuous monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and body temperature
Avoid or minimise adrenaline/sympathomimetics (myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines - arrhythmia risk)
Avoid repeat exposure within about 3 months unless unavoidable; record prior halothane exposures
Have dantrolene and a malignant-hyperthermia protocol immediately available
Resuscitation equipment and antagonists must be on hand
moa: Halothane produces reversible general anaesthesia through dose-dependent depression of the central nervous system. Like other volatile anaesthetics it acts on multiple membrane ion channels and receptors, notably enhancing inhibitory GABA-A and glycine receptor currents and modulating potassium and other channels, reducing neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission. It causes dose-dependent reductions in blood pressure and cardiac output, sensitises the myocardium to catecholamines, depresses respiration, and relaxes uterine and bronchial smooth muscle. A fraction is metabolised in the liver (oxidatively and reductively); reactive trifluoroacetyl metabolites that bind hepatic proteins are implicated in immune-mediated halothane hepatitis.

absolute: History of unexplained jaundice or hepatitis after previous halothane (or other halogenated anaesthetic) exposure
Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia
Known hypersensitivity to halothane or halogenated anaesthetics
relative: Phaeochromocytoma or states with high circulating catecholamines
monitor: Depth of anaesthesia, blood pressure, heart rate/rhythm
Body temperature (early sign of malignant hyperthermia)
Postoperative liver function if hepatotoxicity suspected

preg: Halothane crosses the placenta and is a potent uterine relaxant that can increase blood loss; it depresses the neonate when used near delivery. It should be used in pregnancy only when clearly necessary and administered by experienced anaesthetists, balancing maternal and fetal risks.
lact: Halothane exposure is brief during anaesthesia. Trace amounts may appear in milk; many protocols allow resumption of breastfeeding once the mother has recovered, sometimes discarding milk for a short period. Follow specialist/local guidance.
renal: Halothane undergoes little renal elimination and no specific dose adjustment is required in renal impairment; standard intra-operative monitoring applies.
hepatic: Halothane is associated with two patterns of liver injury: a mild, common, transient transaminase rise, and rare but potentially fatal fulminant immune-mediated halothane hepatitis, the risk of which rises with repeated exposure. It is contraindicated in patients with previous halothane-associated jaundice or hepatitis and should be used cautiously, if at all, in pre-existing liver disease.

major: Adrenaline/sympathomimetic catecholamines - halothane sensitises the myocardium, risking ventricular arrhythmias; limit doses
Other myocardial depressants/QT-prolonging or arrhythmogenic drugs - additive cardiac effects
moderate: Non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers - effect potentiated by halothane
Beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers - additive myocardial depression/hypotension
Aminophylline/theophylline - increased arrhythmia risk with halothane
minor: MAO inhibitors and tricyclics - caution with sympathomimetics under anaesthesia
interactions.food: Not applicable (inhalational anaesthetic; patient is fasted)
interactions.alcohol: Chronic heavy alcohol use may alter anaesthetic requirements; not relevant acutely
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently elevate liver transaminases postoperatively

common: Transient mild rise in liver enzymes
serious: Halothane hepatitis - fulminant hepatic necrosis (rare, potentially fatal)
Cardiac arrhythmias, including ventricular arrhythmias with catecholamines
emergency: Malignant hyperthermia (rising temperature, rigidity, tachycardia, hypercarbia - give dantrolene, stop agent, cool, support)
Refractory ventricular arrhythmia or cardiac arrest

monitoring: Continuous intra-operative monitoring of blood pressure, ECG, oxygenation, capnography and depth of anaesthesia
Core body temperature throughout anaesthesia (malignant hyperthermia)
Postoperative observation for jaundice; check liver function if hepatotoxicity is suspected
Record cumulative halothane exposures to avoid frequent repeat use
counsel: This anaesthetic gas is given by a specialist to keep you asleep and pain-free during surgery
Tell the anaesthetist if you or a blood relative ever had a severe reaction to anaesthesia (very high temperature) or jaundice/liver problems after an operation
Some people feel sick or shivery as the anaesthetic wears off
Report yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine or unusual tiredness in the weeks after surgery
pk: Rapid - smooth inhalational induction within minutes
Anaesthetic effect tracks alveolar/brain partial pressure during administration
Eliminated mainly via the lungs on cessation; about 20% metabolised hepatically
Recovery within minutes of discontinuing the vaporiser as it is exhaled
Store in tightly closed amber bottles, protected from light; contains a thymol stabiliser
pearls: Two signature hazards: immune-mediated HALOTHANE HEPATITIS (risk rises with repeat exposure) and MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA (a recognised trigger - have dantrolene ready)
Avoid repeat halothane within ~3 months and never re-use after previous halothane-associated jaundice/hepatitis
Sensitises the myocardium to catecholamines - limit adrenaline/sympathomimetics to prevent ventricular arrhythmias
Potent uterine relaxant - can increase obstetric/surgical bleeding
Largely replaced by sevoflurane/isoflurane/desflurane in many countries but still used in some settings
openFDA has no current US label; described per BNF/EMA-style monographs and anaesthesia references
missed: Not applicable - halothane is an inhaled anaesthetic administered during a procedure, not a scheduled self-administered medicine.
overdose: Overdose (excessive inspired concentration) causes profound cardiorespiratory depression, hypotension, arrhythmias and apnoea. Management is to discontinue the agent, secure the airway and ventilate with 100% oxygen, and provide cardiovascular support (fluids, vasopressors/inotropes) and arrhythmia treatment until the agent is exhaled.
